title: Across the Sea to Abyssinia
year: Rajab, the fifth year of prophethood — c. 615 CE
teaser: Quraysh sent gifts and two envoys across the sea to have them handed back. The king gave the gifts back.

layers.title: Allah's Earth Is Wide
layers.subtitle: The first time Islam left Arabia
layers.content:
By the middle of the fifth year of prophethood the situation had passed what the weakest believers could carry. Al-Mubarakpuri describes it plainly: the persecution had begun slowly and grown month by month, and the Muslims began looking for a way out of it.

What came down was not a promise of relief in Makkah. It was a reminder that Makkah was not the whole world. Surah az-Zumar was revealed, and in it: «وَأَرْضُ اللَّهِ وَاسِعَةٌ» — 'and Allah's earth is spacious.' (39:10) The verse says that good belongs to those who do good in this world, that the earth is wide, and that the patient will receive their reward without reckoning.

The Prophet ﷺ chose the destination himself, and he chose it on the strength of the man who ruled it. Ashamah, who held the title of Negus, governed Abyssinia across the Red Sea. He was known as a just ruler who did not wrong those under his authority. He was also a Christian, in a Christian kingdom, and the Muslims fleeing to him worshipped no idol and claimed no divinity for a prophet.

So the first organised departure in the history of Islam did not go to a friendly tribe or a sympathetic Arab city. It crossed water, left the peninsula, and put a community of Arabs under the protection of a foreign king who did not share their faith. Nothing in the tribal world they came from had prepared them to expect that this would work.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam; Zad al-Ma'ad 1/24

layers.title: Two Crossings
layers.subtitle: A rumour brought some of them straight back
layers.content:
In Rajab of the fifth year of prophethood, twelve men and four women left. Among them were Uthman ibn Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter. Of those two the Prophet ﷺ said they were the first to migrate in the cause of Allah after Ibrahim and Lut.

They slipped out of Makkah under cover of a dark night and made for the coast, where two boats happened to be sailing for Abyssinia. Word of the departure reached Quraysh and men were sent after them, but the party had already left the port of Shu'aybah. On the far shore they were received warmly and given proper hospitality.

Then came a rumour. In Ramadan of that same year the Prophet ﷺ entered the sanctuary, where a large body of Quraysh notables was sitting, and began reciting Surah an-Najm. They had a habit of shouting over recitation so that no one nearby could follow it. This time they listened, and when he reached the closing command to fall in prostration, they went down with him — unconsciously, in a helpless state, al-Mubarakpuri writes. Those who had not been present rebuked them so severely afterwards that they began inventing explanations for it.

The report that crossed the sea was that the whole of Quraysh had accepted Islam. The emigrants set out for home and arrived in Shawwal. They learned the truth roughly an hour's travel from Makkah. Some turned back to Abyssinia. Others slipped into the city secretly, or entered openly under the protection of some local notable.

The response of Quraysh to news of Abyssinian hospitality was to intensify the treatment of those still in Makkah. So the Prophet ﷺ permitted a second migration. This one was larger and harder to arrange, because Quraysh were now watching for it: eighty-three men and, depending on the version, eighteen or nineteen women. Whether Ammar ibn Yasir was among them the sources leave in doubt.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 53:62 — 'So fall down in prostration to Allah and worship Him alone'
layers.hadith_ref: The prostration in Surah an-Najm — Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas
layers.source: Zad al-Ma'ad 1/24 and 2/44; Ibn Hisham 1/364 — in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Embassy
layers.subtitle: Two envoys, valuable gifts, and a bought court
layers.content:
Quraysh could not accept that a safe haven existed. They sent two men to have the refugees expelled and handed over: Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah, both years away from Islam at that point.

The mission was professionally done. They carried valuable gifts for the king and for his clergy, and before approaching him they won several of his courtiers to their side. Their argument to the throne was framed for a religious ruler: these people had abandoned the religion of their forefathers, and their leader preached a religion that was neither the king's nor theirs.

The Negus did not hand them over. He summoned them and asked them to explain themselves. 'What is this religion that has caused you to separate from your people, and not to enter my religion or any other?'

Ja'far ibn Abi Talib stood up. 'O king, we were an ignorant people. We worshipped idols and ate the meat of dead carcasses. We were accustomed to lewd behaviour, to severing the ties of kinship, neglecting our neighbours, and the strong among us consumed the property of the weak. This is how we were. Then Allah sent a Messenger to us. We knew his lineage, his truthfulness, that he was trustworthy and chaste.'

He listed what the man had commanded: worship of Allah alone, truthful speech, keeping trusts, ties of kinship, kindness to a neighbour, no unlawful bloodshed, prayer, charity, fasting — and what he had forbidden: indecency, obscene speech, consuming an orphan's wealth, slandering chaste women.

Then he described what it had cost. 'Our people rose against us, punishing us, torturing us to get us to leave our religion. So when they overpowered us and came between us and our religion, we came to your land, and chose you over others, hoping that you — O king — will not wrong us.'
layers.source: Ibn Hisham 1/334-338, in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: Surah Maryam in a Christian Court
layers.subtitle: The passage he chose, and why it worked
layers.content:
The Negus asked whether they had with them anything the Messenger had said came from Allah. Ja'far said yes. The king said: recite some of it.

Ja'far recited the opening of Surah Maryam — «وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ مَرْيَمَ» — 'And mention in the Book Maryam.' (19:16) He continued through the account of the births of Yahya and of Isa, down to the passage in which Maryam is fed miraculously. (19:16-33)

He had chosen the one passage in the Qur'an that speaks directly to the court in front of him. A Christian king and his bishops heard Maryam honoured, her son announced, and the child speaking from the cradle to declare himself a servant of Allah given the Book and made a prophet. The king and the bishops wept until the tears ran into the Negus's beard. He said: it seems as if these words and those revealed to Jesus are rays of light radiating from the same source. Then, to the envoys of Quraysh: I cannot give you back these refugees.

They came back the next day with a sharper attack — that the Muslims blasphemed against Jesus. The Muslims were summoned again and asked what they said about him. Ja'far answered: he is the servant of Allah, His Messenger, His spirit and His word breathed into the virgin Maryam. The king said that this was what they themselves believed, told his angry bishops they could fret as they wished, returned the gifts Quraysh had sent, and dismissed the envoys.

One honest note on chronology. Ibn Ishaq places this hearing at the arrival of the emigrants. Other reports say Amr ibn al-As went to the Negus after the Battle of Badr. Some scholars reconcile the two by saying the delegation went on two occasions.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 19:16-33 — the passage recited before the Negus
layers.source: Ibn Hisham 1/334-338, in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: The first time the message was explained to a stranger
layers.content:
The refugees stayed in Abyssinia undisturbed for years, until they left to join the community in Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ later asked the Negus to send Ja'far and his companions back, and they reached him at Khaybar. The Negus himself died in Rajab of the ninth year after the migration; the Prophet ﷺ announced his death and prayed the funeral prayer for him in absentia, from another country.

Three things came out of this crossing.

It established that migration is a legitimate answer. Not surrender, not martyrdom — relocation, undertaken deliberately, with the destination chosen for the character of its ruler rather than the religion of its people. The verse the Muslims carried with them said only that the earth was wide.

It produced the first summary of Islam ever delivered to an outsider. Ja'far did not open with theology or with a demand. He opened with what his people had been — idols, carcasses, broken kinship, the strong eating the property of the weak — and then listed what they had been told to do instead. Prayer and charity are in the list, but so are keeping a trust and being decent to a neighbour. That is how the religion described itself the first time it was asked.

And it showed that the message could be heard by someone who had no stake in Arabia at all. Quraysh brought gifts, courtiers, and a well-built argument, and lost to a recitation. The king wept at a chapter named after Maryam.

What to carry from it is this. Ja'far won that room by telling the plain truth about where he had come from. He did not exaggerate the persecution and he did not soften the ignorance. He described both accurately, and accuracy was enough.
layers.hadith_ref: The funeral prayer in absentia for the Negus — Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Funerals
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: Which verse was revealed pointing the Muslims towards migration?

options.text: 'Allah's earth is spacious' (39:10)
'Emigrate for the sake of your Lord' (74:5)
'And travel through the land' (3:137)
'Flee to Allah' (51:50)

quiz.scholar_reflection: The verse offered no relief in Makkah. It said the earth was wide and that the patient would be rewarded without reckoning. The rest was left to them to arrange.

quiz.prompt: How many left in the first migration, in Rajab of the fifth year of prophethood?

options.text: Eighty-three men and about nineteen women
Twelve men and four women
Seventy men from the Ansar
Forty men and their households

quiz.citation: Zad al-Ma'ad 1/24 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Among them were Uthman ibn Affan and Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter. The second migration was far larger — eighty-three men, and eighteen or nineteen women depending on the report.

quiz.prompt: What false report brought some of the emigrants back from Abyssinia?

options.text: That the Prophet ﷺ had died
That Abu Talib had taken power in Makkah
That the whole of Quraysh had accepted Islam
That the Negus intended to expel them

quiz.citation: Zad al-Ma'ad 1/24; Ibn Hisham 1/364 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: It grew out of a real event. The notables of Quraysh had prostrated when the Prophet ﷺ recited Surah an-Najm in the sanctuary. By the time the story crossed the sea it had become a mass conversion.

quiz.prompt: Which two men did Quraysh send to the Negus to demand the refugees be handed back?

options.text: Abu Jahl and Umayyah ibn Khalaf
Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah
al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah
Abu Sufyan and Suhayl ibn Amr

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/334-338 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Both were still years from Islam. They came with valuable gifts for the king and his clergy, and had won over several courtiers before they ever reached the throne.

quiz.prompt: Which passage did Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recite when the Negus asked to hear some of the revelation?

options.text: The opening of Surah Yusuf
The opening of Surah al-Fatihah
The account of Maryam, Yahya and Isa from Surah Maryam (19:16-33)
The verses of Surah al-Ikhlas

quiz.scholar_reflection: The king and his bishops wept until the tears wet the Negus's beard. He said it seemed these words and those revealed to Jesus were rays of light from the same source.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ sent the most vulnerable Muslims to a Christian king rather than to any Arab ally. What does that choice tell you?

options.text: Justice in a ruler mattered more than shared belief
No Arab tribe could be trusted to defy Quraysh, so the peninsula was not an option
It set a precedent — Muslims may live safely under a non-Muslim authority that does not wrong them
It was a calculated risk taken because the alternative was watching people die

quiz.slider_label: Shared faith or a just ruler
quiz.scholar_reflection: He is described as a just ruler who did not wrong those under him. That was the whole basis on which the safety of the community was staked.

quiz.prompt: Ja'far opened his defence by describing how bad his own people had been — idols, carcasses, broken kinship, the strong consuming the weak. What do you make of starting there?

options.text: It made everything after it credible, because he had not flattered himself first
It explained the change rather than asserting it
It refused the framing Quraysh had used, that these people had abandoned something noble
It is a harder thing to say than a defence of doctrine, and he said it anyway

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/334-338 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He listed prayer and charity alongside keeping a trust and being kind to a neighbour. That is how the religion described itself the first time an outsider asked.

quiz.prompt: Some emigrants returned to Makkah on a rumour, discovered the truth an hour from the city, and had to decide again — go back across the sea, or slip in under someone's protection. How does that sit with you?

options.text: It is the most human moment in the chapter — hope acted on, then withdrawn
They had to make the same hard decision twice, which is harder than making it once
It shows how badly they wanted to go home, and that homesickness is not weakness
Different people chose differently, and the sources do not fault either group

quiz.scholar_reflection: They were an hour's travel from the valley they had grown up in. Some turned round and made for the coast again.

quiz.prompt: Quraysh arrived with gifts, purchased courtiers, and an argument built for a religious king. They were beaten by a recitation. What is the lesson you take?

options.text: Preparation and influence lose to substance when someone finally listens
The Negus was simply an honest man, and honest men are hard to buy
The Qur'an did the work — Ja'far only had to let it be heard
Their whole strategy assumed the king cared about politics more than truth

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/334-338 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He returned their gifts and sent them home. Everything they had spent bought them nothing at the moment it mattered.

quiz.prompt: Migration was permitted for those who could not endure, while others stayed in Makkah under the persecution. Two groups, two paths, neither criticised. What does that tell you about how tests are assigned?

options.text: Endurance and relocation are both legitimate — the wrong one is the one that abandons the faith
People are given what they can carry, and are not measured against each other
Leaving a place that is destroying you is not a retreat from responsibility
The Prophet ﷺ permitted rather than commanded it, leaving the judgement with each person

quiz.scholar_reflection: He permitted it. He did not order it, and he did not go. Both those facts are part of the ruling.
